title: Hyperbolic localized plasmons and twist-induced chirality in an anisotropic 2D material

paper_content.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals materials with strong in-plane anisotropy are emerging as fertile platforms for nanophotonics beyond conventional isotropic noble metals and dielectrics. Here, we demonstrate hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs) in MoOCl2, a representative anisotropic 2D crystal. Unlike conventional plasmons, H-LPRs arise directly from the crystal anisotropy and show unprecedented properties: (i) one-dimensional resonances in circularly symmetric nanodisks, (ii) Z-gap independence in metal–insulator–metal heterostructures, and (iii) twist-induced chirality with circular dichroism values exceeding 0.65. The H-LPRs are characterized by both far-field spectra and near-field imaging. By stacking twisted MoOCl2 flakes, we bridge H-LPRs with concepts of moiré photonics and twistronics, introducing a new degree of freedom in plasmonic design. These findings establish H-LPRs in anisotropic 2D materials as a generalizable and versatile platform for polarization engineering, ultrasensitive chiral sensing, and integration into compact on-chip and quantum nanophotonic devices.
paper_content.introduction:
Chirality and plasmonics underpin a wide range of technologies, from enantioselective sensing1 and drug development2 to photonic information processing3. However, existing plasmonic systems, which are largely based on isotropic noble metals4,5, lack the anisotropy that is required for robust chiral control and tunable light confinement. Light–matter interactions at the nanoscale are often engineered with plasmons in noble metals, which support surface plasmon polaritons6 and localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs)7,8. These modes enable field confinement and applications in sensing9, photocatalysis10,11, and information processing12,13. However, conventional LSPRs are limited by their isotropic permittivity and geometry-dependent resonance tuning.

The rise of layered van der Waals (vdW) materials with novel optical properties has provided new opportunities for nanophotonics14, such as materials with significant anisotropy15, strong nonlinearity16, as well as magnetically-dressed excitons17 and phonon polaritons18–22. Among them, natural hyperbolic materials—van der Waals crystals with anisotropic permittivity components of opposite signs—support hyperbolic polaritons, which are known for sub-wavelength confinement and directional propagation18–30. Hyperbolic polaritons have been widely investigated in phonon materials in the mid-infrared, such as hBN and α-MoO3. Recently, this research has been expanded to plasmon materials in the near-infrared and visible light31–36. However, how hyperbolic dispersion manifests in localized plasmon modes and their distinct properties has remained unexplored.

Here, we experimentally introduce hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs) using layered MoOCl231–36. H-LPRs exhibit distinct properties: (i) one-dimensional resonances in symmetric disk metasurfaces, (ii) Z-gap independence in MoOCl2–insulator–metal stacks, and (iii) twist-induced chirality without breaking geometric symmetry. These unique features enable robust and broadband responses across the visible to near-infrared spectrum. By bridging hyperbolic polaritons and localized plasmons, H-LPRs provide a new nanophotonic toolkit for 2D vdW anisotropic plasmonics and twistronics, with implications for light-field control, polarization engineering, and practical chiral devices.
paper_content.results:
Hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances
MoOCl2 is a layered van der Waals crystal with a monoclinic structure (space group C2/m)31,32 that exhibits pronounced in-plane anisotropy. The structure is strongly coupled along the Mo–O chains, while the inter-chain coupling in the orthogonal direction is significantly weaker. Along the Mo–O chain axis, the material is metallic (εx < 0), whereas the orthogonal directions remain dielectric (εy, εz > 0) across the visible to near-infrared spectrum (Fig. 1a, b)31,34,35,37. This unique permittivity landscape fundamentally distinguishes MoOCl2 from the isotropic noble metals that are typically used in plasmonics. A planar flake with a thickness of tens of nanometers supports hyperbolic plasmon polaritons, whose iso-frequency contours (IFCs) are hyperbolic in the in-plane direction (Fig. 1b), which is expressed as follows:

kx^2/εy + ky^2/εx = ω^2/c^2 (1)

When a MoOCl2 flake is patterned into an anodisk metasurface, a localized resonance mode emerges. The structural parameters, namely, the disk radius (R), thickness (H), and squared period (P), are defined in Fig. 1c. A representative transmission spectrum for R=80nm, H=60nm, and P=500nm under x-polarization shows a distinct resonance peak (Fig. 1d). The corresponding three-dimensional mode distribution (Fig. 1e, f) reveals strong electric fields that are localized at disk edges and surfaces, together with ray-like volumetric profiles inside the structure. Ray-like lines appear because most wavevectors are oriented along the asymptotes of the hyperbola, and their directions are determined by the open angle of the hyperbola. These volumetric ray-like features are hallmarks of hyperbolic dispersion35,38,39 and sharply contrast with the purely surface-confined fields of LSPRs in Au. It should be noted that the full 3D IFCs can be found in the literature33, showing an open-angle 3D hyperboloid. In addition, the ghost mode may have a weak contribution to the in-plane mode distribution33,38,40. More discussions on hyperbolic modes are provided in Supplementary Note 1.

The results of finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations confirm that the mode volume of MoOCl2-based resonances is intrinsically larger than that of Au LSPRs of equivalent geometry. For instance, with the parameters of Fig. 1d, the calculated mode volume is V = ∫ E^2 dV / max(E^2) (2)

using the time-averaged electric field distributions obtained from FDTD calculations. The integration volume covers the entire meta-atom and its near-field region. Here, the ε is omitted due to its anisotropy. The obtained V ≈ 3.5 × 10^-4 λ^3, confirming the strong field confinement of the H-LPR. However, this value is approximately an order of magnitude greater than that of Au LSPRs, which originates from a volumetric hyperbolic distribution rather than surface confinement. Taken together, these results justify the definition of a new class of states, hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs), which bridge the physics of delocalized hyperbolic polaritons and conventional localized plasmons.

To experimentally validate H-LPRs, we fabricated high-quality MoOCl2 nanodisk metasurfaces using electron-beam lithography and reactive ion etching, following iterative optimization. A representative scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image reveals homogeneous morphology across large areas (R=87nm, H=50nm, and P=500nm) (Fig. 2b). Optical images under reflective microscopy further highlight the anisotropy: under x-polarization, the disks exhibit a metallic golden luster, whereas under y-polarization they appear as dielectric films (Fig. 2c). Each metasurface array spans 50 μm × 50 μm with a designed disk radius. Unless otherwise specified, the x-polarization is aligned with the metallic chain axis.

The transmission spectra reveal clear resonances under x-polarization that redshift systematically with increasing disk radius (Fig. 2d). In sharp contrast, no resonance peaks are observed under y-polarization, where high transmittance persists across all disk sizes (Fig. 2e). To more precisely probe the polarization dependence, we measured the spectra as the polarizer was rotated from –90° to +90° (Fig. 2f). The corresponding differential spectra |T – T90°| highlight the resonance evolution, and the peak intensity variation follows Malus’s law (I = I0 cos^2 θ) (Fig. 2g, h). This angular dependence provides direct experimental evidence for the one-dimensional characteristic of the H-LPR mode, and the extinction ratio between x- and y-polarized excitations at 840 nm is approximately 11.5, confirming that the resonance is purely one-dimensional along the anisotropic axis.

FDTD simulations reproduce all of the observed spectral features, and further experiments on samples with various thicknesses and fabrication conditions confirm the reproducibility and robustness of the results (Supplementary Figs. 4–7). Importantly, this intrinsic one-dimensionality arises despite the highly circularly symmetric disk geometry and originates solely from the in-plane anisotropic permittivity of MoOCl2. Such 1D resonances in symmetric geometries open new opportunities for light-field control and polarization-sensitive detection and may be further engineered for mode coupling and modulation, as demonstrated in metallic LSPRs13,41,42 and dielectric metasurfaces43.

To further investigate the resonance properties of H-LPRs, we performed near-field characterizations using photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM) integrated with a tunable femtosecond laser beamline. This method has previously been used in the study of various near-field modes supported by metals and dielectrics8,41,44–48. The laser beam was incident at the normal angle, with the polarization controlled by a λ/2 waveplate. Near-field imaging in the near-infrared using PEEM relies on a multi-photon photoemission process to overcome the material’s work function. The nonlinear photoemission yield follows PE ∝ IN, where PE is the photoemission intensity, I is the local light intensity, and N is the nonlinear order (here, N = 4, as measured).

As shown in Fig. 3a, under x-polarization, the PEEM images exhibit strong photoemission signals, indicating the strong near-field enhancement of the localized modes (see enlarged PEEM images in Supplementary Fig. 8). In contrast, almost no signals can be observed under y-polarization. Sweeping the excitation wavelengths under constant laser power enables the photoemission yield spectra (near-field enhancement spectra) to be obtained. As illustrated in Fig. 3b, the near-field spectra are consistent with the far-field transmission spectra for both x- and y-polarizations, providing robust evidence for the 1D localized resonance characteristic of MoOCl2 disks.

Z-gap independence in metal–insulator–metal structures
To probe the out-of-plane response of H-LPRs, we fabricated MoOCl2/Al2O3/Au metal–insulator–metal (MIM) structures with controlled Al2O3 spacer thicknesses from 2.5 to 20 nm via atomic layer deposition (Fig. 4a–c). In conventional Au-based MIM systems, the resonance frequency strongly depends on the gap thickness because of the formation of highly confined gap modes. In contrast, the resonance wavelengths of the MoOCl2 MIMs remain nearly constant across this entire range of spacer thicknesses. The evolution of the peak wavelengths of the reflection spectra with increasing Al2O3 gap size (Fig. 4d) clearly demonstrates this invariance, thus establishing Z-gap independence as an intrinsic property of MoOCl2 H-LPRs.

Quantitatively, the resonance shift versus spacer thickness yields |dλ/dG| < 1.5 nm from 2.5 to 20 nm for MoOCl2 H-LPRs, whereas it reaches 101–102 nm for Au MIMs, clearly demonstrating the pronounced Z-gap independence. The results of numerical simulations corroborate the experimental data and clarify the physical mechanism (Fig. 4e). Along the z-axis, MoOCl2 has a positive permittivity (εz > 0)31 that closely matches that of Al2O3 (Fig. 4f), thereby suppressing the high-k gap modes that are responsible for the strong thickness dependence of noble-metal MIMs (Fig. 4g) (More discussion on gap mode versus z-axis permittivity are shown in Supplementary Note 6). In Au MIMs, the abrupt permittivity discontinuity across the spacer leads to strongly localized, thickness-sensitive resonances (Fig. 4g)49. The absence of such discontinuity in MoOCl2 explains the observed robustness. Importantly, compared with MoOCl2 disks directly on glass substrates, MIM structures exhibit resonance redshifts to longer wavelengths (e.g., an ~100 nm redshift for R=60 nm), which expands the spectral tunability of H-LPRs.

This Z-gap independence is technologically significant. It removes sensitivity to nanometer-scale fabrication tolerances, which is a common bottleneck for reproducible nanophotonic devices. Moreover, it enables scalable stacking of metasurfaces and heterostructures without precise spacer control, thereby facilitating the integration of H-LPRs into complex photonic architectures. Further comparisons of the spectral line shapes that confirm the invariance are provided in Supplementary Fig. 9.

Twist chirality in symmetric geometries
Chirality can be achieved by breaking the mirror symmetry of a structure. Various strategies, such as the assembly of unit structures by in-plane rotation5, the introduction of vertical tilt50,51 and structural twisting52–54, have been employed to construct chiral responses. Having established the 1D anisotropy and Z-gap independence, we sought to realize optical chirality by twisting the in-plane anisotropic permittivity axes of stacked MoOCl2 disks while maintaining circular symmetry (as illustrated in Fig. 5a). SEM and optical microscopy confirm high-quality fabrication with uniform alignment and negligible defects (Fig. 5b, c). Under left- and right-circularly polarized (LCP and RCP) excitation, the transmission spectra reveal resonance peak shifts that exceed 100 nm (Fig. 5d), and the corresponding circular dichroism (CD) values are >0.2, where CD is defined as CD = (TLCP − TRCP) / (TLCP + TRCP)51. These values are remarkable considering the fully symmetric disk geometry and rival or surpass those of engineered chiral metasurfaces that rely on explicit geometric asymmetry.

Simulations reproduce the experimental chirality and reveal its robustness against variations in the twist angle, thickness mismatch, and disk radius (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Note 7). For example, even when the upper and lower disk thicknesses deviate by tens of nanometers, the chiral response remains substantial (Supplementary Fig. 14). This robustness is consistent with an effective thickness model, in which LCP and RCP waves accumulate different optical path lengths because of opposite polarization rotations (Supplementary Note 7). The model predicts that the total effective thickness governs the degree of chirality, which explains why deviations in individual disk dimensions do not strongly reduce the effect. As shown in Fig. 5f, the different rotations of near-field modes when passing through the twist disks can be observed, for LCP and RCP light.

Beyond its robustness, twist-induced chirality is broadband and persists across visible to near-infrared wavelengths. Moreover, the metasurfaces support tunable polarization responses across the full Poincaré sphere by adjusting the twist parameters, thereby enabling complete polarization engineering (Fig. 5f). This functionality establishes H-LPR-based twist metasurfaces as promising platforms for ultrasensitive chiral sensing, broadband polarization control, and spin–photon interfaces. Detailed simulation studies of the twist angle dependence and experimental spectra from multiple samples with various thicknesses and radii are presented in (Supplementary Notes 7 and 8), which support the robustness of the chiral response, and the reproducibility was confirmed over five independent samples fabricated on separate substrates.

It should be noted that the present study does not intend to achieve the optimal chiral response. By designing the metasurface period, the in-plane geometric shape and the vertical multilayer stacking, it is possible to further engineer the chiral response. For example, the circular dichroism can be improved by reducing the metasurface period, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 21. The maximum circular dichroism exceeds 0.65 in simulations and 0.54 in experiments (P=350 nm). The CD enhancement arises from the increased density and stronger near-field coupling between adjacent disks as the period decreases, which effectively amplifies the asymmetric local field for LCP and RCP excitation. In addition, the comparisons of twisted MoOCl2 metasurfaces with twisted noble metal metasurfaces and twisted unpatterned MoOCl2 films are discussed in Supplementary Note 8.
paper_content.methods:
Sample fabrication and characterizations
The MoOCl2 flakes were mechanically exfoliated on polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) sheets from bulk crystals (Nanjing MKNANO Tech. Co., Ltd. (www.mukenano.com)), and the thicknesses of the MoOCl2 flakes were estimated by the reflected color under optical microscopy before transfer. The selected MoOCl2 flakes were transferred onto a substrate using the all-dry transfer method under optical microscopy. For single–disk and twist metasurfaces, soda-lime glass substrates with a ~10 nm ITO layer were used. For MIM metasurfaces, silica substrates were used. Each substrate was pre-marked with gold markers for positioning.

For single–disk metasurfaces, the usual process flow mainly includes electron-beam lithography (EBL) and reactive ion etching (RIE), with EB resist as a mask. Before EBL, an EB resist (ZEP520A:ZEP-A=1:1, Zeon Chemicals) was spin-coated onto the substrate with MoOCl2 flakes at 300 rpm for 3 s and 3000 rpm for 60 s. Next, the substrate was pre-baked at 180 °C for 2 min. The EBL system (ELS-F130HM, Elionix) operated at 130 kV with an electron current of 100 pA. After EBL, the sample was developed with ZED-N50 for 60 s and ZED-B for 10 s. Then, RIE (RIE-101iPH, Samco Inc.) was used to etch the MoOCl2 with SF6 gas. After RIE, the EB resist was cleanly removed using the lift-off (DMAC) process at 70°C for 20–30 min, without ultrasonication. Finally, the sample was cleaned with acetone and methanol. We also fabricated some samples with a hard mask of several-nm Ti. For those samples, a helicon sputtering (MPS-4000C1/HC1, ULVAC) and an ultrasonic lift-off process were used before the RIE process.

For twist metasurfaces, MoOCl2 flakes with similar thickness were pre-selected, and the twist angle was pre-defined during the transfer process. The surface of the lower MoOCl2 was cleaned to remove residue PDMS. After transfer, the sample was annealed under vacuum at 100–130°C for 20 min. These steps were intended to reduce interlayer bubbles. The subsequent steps are the same as those for single–disk metasurfaces with EB resist as a mask.

For MoOCl2 MIM metasurfaces, silica substrates with gold markers were used to sputter 100 nm Au, with 2 nm Ti as the adhesion layer. Then, Al2O3 layers were grown on the substrates using atomic layer deposition (ALD) at a rate of 1 nm/10 cycles (R-200 advanced, Picosun). Then, MoOCl2 flakes were transferred onto these Al2O3/Au/SiO2 substrates. The subsequent steps are the same as those for single–disk metasurfaces with EB resist as a mask.

After sample preparations, the samples were characterized using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (SU8230, Hitachi High-Technologies), and a thickness measuring instrument (ET200, Kosaka Laboratory, Ltd.).

Spectral measurements
The resonance modes of MoOCl2 metasurfaces were characterized using transmission or reflection spectra, with a home-built optical microscopy system equipped with a photonic multichannel analyzer (PMAC7473, Hamamatsu Photonics). A linear polarizer and a 1/4 λ waveplate were used to control the polarization states. For the reflection spectra, a silver mirror was used as the reference, and calibration was performed using the reflectance of silicon to obtain the actual spectra.

PEEM measurements
The PEEM measurements were performed on a high-resolution low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM)/PEEM system (ACSPELEEM III, Elmitec GmbH). A commercial Ti:sapphire femtosecond laser (MaiTai HP, Spectra-Physics, pulse duration: 80−100 fs) operated at 690−1040 nm (2.9 W @ 820 nm) with a repetition rate of 80 MHz was used to provide a tunable laser for PEEM measurements. The pulses were focused on the sample surface at normal incidence with a spot diameter of approximately 100 μm. The polarization of the laser was controlled by a λ/2 waveplate.

Simulations
The resonance modes of MoOCl2 metasurfaces were simulated using the finite-difference time-domain method (FDTD, Ansys Lumerical), using the measured permittivity (εx, εy) and theoretical permittivity (εz). The optical properties of Au were obtained from Johnson and Christy and the refractive index of the glass substrate was set to 1.5. For twist metasurfaces, the refractive index axes were rotated using the “permittivity rotation attribute” component. The excitation light was set to normal incidence with the required polarization states. The FDTD simulations well reproduced the experimental results.

Data availability
The data supporting the findings are displayed in the main text and the supplementary information. All raw data are available from the corresponding authors upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Li et al. describes the nanofabrication and investigation of arrays of nanostructured MoOCl2 realizing both hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances as well as chiral optical responses. Hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances have never been reported prior to this work and suggest a new opportunity for controlling and modifying MoOCl2 for nanophotonic applications. They authors also demonstrate that by creating at twisted MoOCl2 sample prior to nanofabrication they can achieve extremely strong circular dichroism even in a material that is otherwise isotropic in plane. Such research into anisotropic and hyperbolic materials, such as MoOCl2, is extremely important in the nanophotonics field as efforts have turned to using natural material anisotropy in order to control material properties.
Overall the manuscript was well written, the analysis, interpretation and conclusions were largely sound. However, there are several additional major and minor points that should be addressed in revisions.
Major Points:
1. The authors should address what benefits the twisted MoOCl2 provides over chiral noble metal nanostructures.
2. The authors should be careful to note that in a biaxial medium there are always two propagating wave solutions (both extraordinary). The hyperbolic modes occur for only one root of the quartic wave equation. Do both roots play a role in the observed modes in the H-LPRs? (see Narimanov, E. E. Phys. Rev. A 98, 013818 (2018))
3. In the text the manuscript states: "Ray-like lines appear because most wavevectors are oriented along the asymptotes of the hyperbola, and their directions are determined by the open angle of the hyperbola.”
These ray-like modes seem to be attributed to “ghost modes” else where. See Narimanov, E. E. Phys. Rev. A 98, 013818 (2018) and Venturi et al. Such directional ghost modes show the unique character of having both propagating and evanescent character even without intrinsic material losses. Are the rays observed here due to the hyperbolic modes (defined by the hyperbolic isofrequency surface) or the ghost modes? I don't disagree that that these appear to be localized plasmon resonances in a hyperbolic material, the question becomes do they have truly hyperbolic dispersion or not.
4. As discussed in the supplementary information increasing R redshifts the spectra while increasing H blueshifts the spectra. Could the authors explain why increasing H would increase the energy of the hyperbolic mode? It seems that thin film models of surface plasmonic behavior could explain this in a quite straightforward fashion without needing to invoke a hyperbolic mode.
Minor Points:
1. Figures 2d and e, please clarify more in the figure itself that the spectra are being plotted versus disk radius.
2. Figure 3 is confusing. It was hard to tell which of the subpanels were which polarizations and smaller FOVs at first glance. I would recommend modifying the arrangement of the panels and perhaps being more selective on which panels are displayed in the main text.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Comments about NCOMMS-25-92838-T
In this work, the authors report hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances in the two-dimensional material MoOCl2, which exhibits strong in-plane anisotropy, and introduce twist-induced chirality in geometrically symmetric metasurfaces. The observed plasmon resonances feature one-dimensional confinement, z-gap independence, and pronounced circular dichroism arising from twist-induced chirality. However, promising hyperbolic media are expected to exhibit high electromagnetic confinement, low energy loss, and flexible tunability under external fields. The hyperbolic MoOCl2 system does not offer any fundamentally new advantages in electromagnetic confinement, energy loss and tunability, compared with previously reported materials such as MoO3, h-BN, WTe2, Ga2O3 and black phosphorus, all of which have already been extensively studied for supporting hyperbolic polaritons. In addition, the current experimental data set is incomplete and insufficient to support the major claims making it difficult to evaluate the robustness of the conclusions. As a result, the novelty of this work appears limited for publication in Nature Communications and would be more suitable for a specialized journal.
Comments:
1. The authors claim that MoOCl₂ exhibits one-dimensional characteristics in its hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances. However, one-dimensional materials are generally composed of 1D structural units connected by weak van der Waals interactions, which is not clearly illustrated or discussed in Fig. 1a. Clarification on the structural origin of this claimed one-dimensionality is necessary.
2. In Fig. 1b, the real part of the permittivity appears to vary almost linearly with wavelength, which seems unusual for 2D materials. It would be necessary to also provide the imaginary part of the optical dielectric function, as the real and imaginary components should satisfy the Kramers–Kronig relation. Including this information would help verify the physical consistency of the presented optical data. If experimental measurements are challenging, first-principles calculations could also be provided to support and better interpret the observed results.
3. The physical origin of the observed hyperbolicity should be clarified. In particular, the respective roles of interband and intraband transitions, which are crucial for producing strong optical anisotropy and hyperbolic dispersion, need to be discussed in greater detail. Providing this analysis would help elucidate the microscopic mechanism underlying the reported hyperbolic behavior. Similar discussions has been reported in Nat Commun 11, 1158 (2020).
4. The presented hyperbolic isofrequency contours appear incomplete. Additional data points at a wider range of frequencies should be included to clearly illustrate the frequency range over which hyperbolicity occurs, as well as the transition from elliptic to hyperbolic dispersion. This would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the material's optical anisotropy and dispersion characteristics.
5. The wavelength ratio of the hyperbolic in-plane dispersion to the corresponding free-space photon wavelength (i.e., electromagnetic confinement) should be provided, along with the propagation length and lifetime of the hyperbolic polaritons. These parameters are essential for quantitatively evaluating the performance and quality of hyperbolic materials.
6. Plasmon hyperbolic materials often exhibit higher losses, a short discussion on loss mechanisms in MoOCl2, including thickness dependence and Q-factor of H-LPRs would help readers assess performance limits and potential device implications.
7. The manuscript states that chirality is robust to thickness mismatch and fabrication variations, but it would help to quantify the tolerance (percent-level deviations in thickness or twist angle).
8. Can the authors elaborate on the microscopic origin of the twist-induced chirality, possibly through a brief tensor-transformation argument for the rotated permittivity?
9. Would chirality persist in multilayer twist stacks (beyond bilayers), and if so, does the effective thickness model remain applicable?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript reports the discovery and experimental demonstration of the hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs) in the anisotropic two-dimensional van der Waals material MoOCl₂. H-LPRs originate from the intrinsic in-plane anisotropic permittivity (metallic along the Mo-O chain axis, dielectric in orthogonal directions), leading to hyperbolic iso-frequency contours. H-LPRs exhibit three important properties: one-dimensional resonance, Z-gap independence and twist-induced chirality. These properties are validated through far-field spectroscopy, near-field photoemission electron microscopy imaging, and comprehensive simulations. Overall, the manuscript is clearly written and the topic is of interest. However, prior to publication, several issues should be addressed:
1.The authors attribute Z-gap independence to the matching permittivity between MoOCl₂ and Al₂O₃. Could a more quantitative analysis be provided to explain why the high-k gap modes is strongly suppressed, leading to insensitivity to gap thickness?
2.For anisotropic 2D materials (e.g., α-MoO₃), studies have shown that significant circular dichroism can be achieved by directly stacking two flakes with a twist angle. If two pristine, unpatterned MoOCl₂ flakes are stacked with a twist, what would be the expected CD value of such a system? Is fabricating a metasurface to obtain H-LPRs a necessary condition for achieving the strong chirality?
3.To demonstrate hyperbolic properties, the inset in Fig. 1b only emphasizes the hyperbolic in-plane isofrequency contours (xy-plane). However, in Fig. 1f, the ray-like electric field distribution, which is a hallmark of hyperbolicity, appears to be stronger out-of-plane (xz-plane). Does this suggest that the one-dimensional resonance characteristic stems from both in-plane and out-of-plane hyperbolic properties?
4.Lines 78-80 of the manuscript state: "These volumetric ray-like features are...sharply contrast with the purely surface-confined fields of LSPRs in Au." For a more intuitive and direct comparison, it would be helpful to provide simulated electric field distributions for Au LSPRs.
5.In the introduction, when discussing hyperbolic polaritons, the reviewer recommends citing Nature Communications 11, 1158 (2020), which reports WTe₂ as another hyperbolic material and is relevant to the context.

Reply to 3.6: The loss of material itself is correlated with the imaginary part of
permittivity, which behaves as the absorption of the material, involving interband and
intraband transitions. For nanostructures, except for absorption loss, radiative decay
(also called scattering decay) is another pathway. That is to say, the decay pathway of
localized plasmons supported by MoOCl nanostructures includes both absorption loss
2
and radiative decay. The former depends on the material itself; the latter depends on
the design of the nanostructures, including their geometric size and shape, the
metasurface period and the dielectric environment (J. Chem. Phys. 153, 120902 (2020);
Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 163901 (2020)). For example, the radiative decay rate is positively

## Abstract

Two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals materials with strong in-plane anisotropy are emerging as fertile platforms for nanophotonics beyond conventional isotropic noble metals and dielectrics. Here, we demonstrate hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs) in MoOCl2, a representative anisotropic 2D crystal. Unlike conventional plasmons, H-LPRs arise directly from the crystal anisotropy and show unprecedented properties: (i) one-dimensional resonances in circularly symmetric nanodisks, (ii) Z-gap independence in metal–insulator–metal heterostructures, and (iii) twist-induced chirality with circular dichroism values exceeding 0.65. The H-LPRs are characterized by both far-field spectra and near-field imaging. By stacking twisted MoOCl2 flakes, we bridge H-LPRs with concepts of moiré photonics and twistronics, introducing a new degree of freedom in plasmonic design. These findings establish H-LPRs in anisotropic 2D materials as a generalizable and versatile platform for polarization engineering, ultrasensitive chiral sensing, and integration into compact on-chip and quantum nanophotonic devices.

---

## Introduction

Chirality and plasmonics underpin a wide range of technologies, from enantioselective sensing1 and drug development2 to photonic information processing3. However, existing plasmonic systems, which are largely based on isotropic noble metals4,5, lack the anisotropy that is required for robust chiral control and tunable light confinement. Light–matter interactions at the nanoscale are often engineered with plasmons in noble metals, which support surface plasmon polaritons6 and localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs)7,8. These modes enable field confinement and applications in sensing9, photocatalysis10,11, and information processing12,13. However, conventional LSPRs are limited by their isotropic permittivity and geometry-dependent resonance tuning.

The rise of layered van der Waals (vdW) materials with novel optical properties has provided new opportunities for nanophotonics14, such as materials with significant anisotropy15, strong nonlinearity16, as well as magnetically-dressed excitons17 and phonon polaritons18–22. Among them, natural hyperbolic materials—van der Waals crystals with anisotropic permittivity components of opposite signs—support hyperbolic polaritons, which are known for sub-wavelength confinement and directional propagation18–30. Hyperbolic polaritons have been widely investigated in phonon materials in the mid-infrared, such as hBN and α-MoO3. Recently, this research has been expanded to plasmon materials in the near-infrared and visible light31–36. However, how hyperbolic dispersion manifests in localized plasmon modes and their distinct properties has remained unexplored.

Here, we experimentally introduce hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs) using layered MoOCl231–36. H-LPRs exhibit distinct properties: (i) one-dimensional resonances in symmetric disk metasurfaces, (ii) Z-gap independence in MoOCl2–insulator–metal stacks, and (iii) twist-induced chirality without breaking geometric symmetry. These unique features enable robust and broadband responses across the visible to near-infrared spectrum. By bridging hyperbolic polaritons and localized plasmons, H-LPRs provide a new nanophotonic toolkit for 2D vdW anisotropic plasmonics and twistronics, with implications for light-field control, polarization engineering, and practical chiral devices.

---

## Results

Hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances
MoOCl2 is a layered van der Waals crystal with a monoclinic structure (space group C2/m)31,32 that exhibits pronounced in-plane anisotropy. The structure is strongly coupled along the Mo–O chains, while the inter-chain coupling in the orthogonal direction is significantly weaker. Along the Mo–O chain axis, the material is metallic (εx < 0), whereas the orthogonal directions remain dielectric (εy, εz > 0) across the visible to near-infrared spectrum (Fig. 1a, b)31,34,35,37. This unique permittivity landscape fundamentally distinguishes MoOCl2 from the isotropic noble metals that are typically used in plasmonics. A planar flake with a thickness of tens of nanometers supports hyperbolic plasmon polaritons, whose iso-frequency contours (IFCs) are hyperbolic in the in-plane direction (Fig. 1b), which is expressed as follows:

kx^2/εy + ky^2/εx = ω^2/c^2 (1)

When a MoOCl2 flake is patterned into an anodisk metasurface, a localized resonance mode emerges. The structural parameters, namely, the disk radius (R), thickness (H), and squared period (P), are defined in Fig. 1c. A representative transmission spectrum for R=80nm, H=60nm, and P=500nm under x-polarization shows a distinct resonance peak (Fig. 1d). The corresponding three-dimensional mode distribution (Fig. 1e, f) reveals strong electric fields that are localized at disk edges and surfaces, together with ray-like volumetric profiles inside the structure. Ray-like lines appear because most wavevectors are oriented along the asymptotes of the hyperbola, and their directions are determined by the open angle of the hyperbola. These volumetric ray-like features are hallmarks of hyperbolic dispersion35,38,39 and sharply contrast with the purely surface-confined fields of LSPRs in Au. It should be noted that the full 3D IFCs can be found in the literature33, showing an open-angle 3D hyperboloid. In addition, the ghost mode may have a weak contribution to the in-plane mode distribution33,38,40. More discussions on hyperbolic modes are provided in Supplementary Note 1.

The results of finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations confirm that the mode volume of MoOCl2-based resonances is intrinsically larger than that of Au LSPRs of equivalent geometry. For instance, with the parameters of Fig. 1d, the calculated mode volume is V = ∫ E^2 dV / max(E^2) (2)

using the time-averaged electric field distributions obtained from FDTD calculations. The integration volume covers the entire meta-atom and its near-field region. Here, the ε is omitted due to its anisotropy. The obtained V ≈ 3.5 × 10^-4 λ^3, confirming the strong field confinement of the H-LPR. However, this value is approximately an order of magnitude greater than that of Au LSPRs, which originates from a volumetric hyperbolic distribution rather than surface confinement. Taken together, these results justify the definition of a new class of states, hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs), which bridge the physics of delocalized hyperbolic polaritons and conventional localized plasmons.

To experimentally validate H-LPRs, we fabricated high-quality MoOCl2 nanodisk metasurfaces using electron-beam lithography and reactive ion etching, following iterative optimization. A representative scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image reveals homogeneous morphology across large areas (R=87nm, H=50nm, and P=500nm) (Fig. 2b). Optical images under reflective microscopy further highlight the anisotropy: under x-polarization, the disks exhibit a metallic golden luster, whereas under y-polarization they appear as dielectric films (Fig. 2c). Each metasurface array spans 50 μm × 50 μm with a designed disk radius. Unless otherwise specified, the x-polarization is aligned with the metallic chain axis.

The transmission spectra reveal clear resonances under x-polarization that redshift systematically with increasing disk radius (Fig. 2d). In sharp contrast, no resonance peaks are observed under y-polarization, where high transmittance persists across all disk sizes (Fig. 2e). To more precisely probe the polarization dependence, we measured the spectra as the polarizer was rotated from –90° to +90° (Fig. 2f). The corresponding differential spectra |T – T90°| highlight the resonance evolution, and the peak intensity variation follows Malus’s law (I = I0 cos^2 θ) (Fig. 2g, h). This angular dependence provides direct experimental evidence for the one-dimensional characteristic of the H-LPR mode, and the extinction ratio between x- and y-polarized excitations at 840 nm is approximately 11.5, confirming that the resonance is purely one-dimensional along the anisotropic axis.

FDTD simulations reproduce all of the observed spectral features, and further experiments on samples with various thicknesses and fabrication conditions confirm the reproducibility and robustness of the results (Supplementary Figs. 4–7). Importantly, this intrinsic one-dimensionality arises despite the highly circularly symmetric disk geometry and originates solely from the in-plane anisotropic permittivity of MoOCl2. Such 1D resonances in symmetric geometries open new opportunities for light-field control and polarization-sensitive detection and may be further engineered for mode coupling and modulation, as demonstrated in metallic LSPRs13,41,42 and dielectric metasurfaces43.

To further investigate the resonance properties of H-LPRs, we performed near-field characterizations using photoemission electron microscopy (PEEM) integrated with a tunable femtosecond laser beamline. This method has previously been used in the study of various near-field modes supported by metals and dielectrics8,41,44–48. The laser beam was incident at the normal angle, with the polarization controlled by a λ/2 waveplate. Near-field imaging in the near-infrared using PEEM relies on a multi-photon photoemission process to overcome the material’s work function. The nonlinear photoemission yield follows PE ∝ IN, where PE is the photoemission intensity, I is the local light intensity, and N is the nonlinear order (here, N = 4, as measured).

As shown in Fig. 3a, under x-polarization, the PEEM images exhibit strong photoemission signals, indicating the strong near-field enhancement of the localized modes (see enlarged PEEM images in Supplementary Fig. 8). In contrast, almost no signals can be observed under y-polarization. Sweeping the excitation wavelengths under constant laser power enables the photoemission yield spectra (near-field enhancement spectra) to be obtained. As illustrated in Fig. 3b, the near-field spectra are consistent with the far-field transmission spectra for both x- and y-polarizations, providing robust evidence for the 1D localized resonance characteristic of MoOCl2 disks.

Z-gap independence in metal–insulator–metal structures
To probe the out-of-plane response of H-LPRs, we fabricated MoOCl2/Al2O3/Au metal–insulator–metal (MIM) structures with controlled Al2O3 spacer thicknesses from 2.5 to 20 nm via atomic layer deposition (Fig. 4a–c). In conventional Au-based MIM systems, the resonance frequency strongly depends on the gap thickness because of the formation of highly confined gap modes. In contrast, the resonance wavelengths of the MoOCl2 MIMs remain nearly constant across this entire range of spacer thicknesses. The evolution of the peak wavelengths of the reflection spectra with increasing Al2O3 gap size (Fig. 4d) clearly demonstrates this invariance, thus establishing Z-gap independence as an intrinsic property of MoOCl2 H-LPRs.

Quantitatively, the resonance shift versus spacer thickness yields |dλ/dG| < 1.5 nm from 2.5 to 20 nm for MoOCl2 H-LPRs, whereas it reaches 101–102 nm for Au MIMs, clearly demonstrating the pronounced Z-gap independence. The results of numerical simulations corroborate the experimental data and clarify the physical mechanism (Fig. 4e). Along the z-axis, MoOCl2 has a positive permittivity (εz > 0)31 that closely matches that of Al2O3 (Fig. 4f), thereby suppressing the high-k gap modes that are responsible for the strong thickness dependence of noble-metal MIMs (Fig. 4g) (More discussion on gap mode versus z-axis permittivity are shown in Supplementary Note 6). In Au MIMs, the abrupt permittivity discontinuity across the spacer leads to strongly localized, thickness-sensitive resonances (Fig. 4g)49. The absence of such discontinuity in MoOCl2 explains the observed robustness. Importantly, compared with MoOCl2 disks directly on glass substrates, MIM structures exhibit resonance redshifts to longer wavelengths (e.g., an ~100 nm redshift for R=60 nm), which expands the spectral tunability of H-LPRs.

This Z-gap independence is technologically significant. It removes sensitivity to nanometer-scale fabrication tolerances, which is a common bottleneck for reproducible nanophotonic devices. Moreover, it enables scalable stacking of metasurfaces and heterostructures without precise spacer control, thereby facilitating the integration of H-LPRs into complex photonic architectures. Further comparisons of the spectral line shapes that confirm the invariance are provided in Supplementary Fig. 9.

Twist chirality in symmetric geometries
Chirality can be achieved by breaking the mirror symmetry of a structure. Various strategies, such as the assembly of unit structures by in-plane rotation5, the introduction of vertical tilt50,51 and structural twisting52–54, have been employed to construct chiral responses. Having established the 1D anisotropy and Z-gap independence, we sought to realize optical chirality by twisting the in-plane anisotropic permittivity axes of stacked MoOCl2 disks while maintaining circular symmetry (as illustrated in Fig. 5a). SEM and optical microscopy confirm high-quality fabrication with uniform alignment and negligible defects (Fig. 5b, c). Under left- and right-circularly polarized (LCP and RCP) excitation, the transmission spectra reveal resonance peak shifts that exceed 100 nm (Fig. 5d), and the corresponding circular dichroism (CD) values are >0.2, where CD is defined as CD = (TLCP − TRCP) / (TLCP + TRCP)51. These values are remarkable considering the fully symmetric disk geometry and rival or surpass those of engineered chiral metasurfaces that rely on explicit geometric asymmetry.

Simulations reproduce the experimental chirality and reveal its robustness against variations in the twist angle, thickness mismatch, and disk radius (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Note 7). For example, even when the upper and lower disk thicknesses deviate by tens of nanometers, the chiral response remains substantial (Supplementary Fig. 14). This robustness is consistent with an effective thickness model, in which LCP and RCP waves accumulate different optical path lengths because of opposite polarization rotations (Supplementary Note 7). The model predicts that the total effective thickness governs the degree of chirality, which explains why deviations in individual disk dimensions do not strongly reduce the effect. As shown in Fig. 5f, the different rotations of near-field modes when passing through the twist disks can be observed, for LCP and RCP light.

Beyond its robustness, twist-induced chirality is broadband and persists across visible to near-infrared wavelengths. Moreover, the metasurfaces support tunable polarization responses across the full Poincaré sphere by adjusting the twist parameters, thereby enabling complete polarization engineering (Fig. 5f). This functionality establishes H-LPR-based twist metasurfaces as promising platforms for ultrasensitive chiral sensing, broadband polarization control, and spin–photon interfaces. Detailed simulation studies of the twist angle dependence and experimental spectra from multiple samples with various thicknesses and radii are presented in (Supplementary Notes 7 and 8), which support the robustness of the chiral response, and the reproducibility was confirmed over five independent samples fabricated on separate substrates.

It should be noted that the present study does not intend to achieve the optimal chiral response. By designing the metasurface period, the in-plane geometric shape and the vertical multilayer stacking, it is possible to further engineer the chiral response. For example, the circular dichroism can be improved by reducing the metasurface period, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 21. The maximum circular dichroism exceeds 0.65 in simulations and 0.54 in experiments (P=350 nm). The CD enhancement arises from the increased density and stronger near-field coupling between adjacent disks as the period decreases, which effectively amplifies the asymmetric local field for LCP and RCP excitation. In addition, the comparisons of twisted MoOCl2 metasurfaces with twisted noble metal metasurfaces and twisted unpatterned MoOCl2 films are discussed in Supplementary Note 8.

---

## Methods

Sample fabrication and characterizations
The MoOCl2 flakes were mechanically exfoliated on polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) sheets from bulk crystals (Nanjing MKNANO Tech. Co., Ltd. (www.mukenano.com)), and the thicknesses of the MoOCl2 flakes were estimated by the reflected color under optical microscopy before transfer. The selected MoOCl2 flakes were transferred onto a substrate using the all-dry transfer method under optical microscopy. For single–disk and twist metasurfaces, soda-lime glass substrates with a ~10 nm ITO layer were used. For MIM metasurfaces, silica substrates were used. Each substrate was pre-marked with gold markers for positioning.

For single–disk metasurfaces, the usual process flow mainly includes electron-beam lithography (EBL) and reactive ion etching (RIE), with EB resist as a mask. Before EBL, an EB resist (ZEP520A:ZEP-A=1:1, Zeon Chemicals) was spin-coated onto the substrate with MoOCl2 flakes at 300 rpm for 3 s and 3000 rpm for 60 s. Next, the substrate was pre-baked at 180 °C for 2 min. The EBL system (ELS-F130HM, Elionix) operated at 130 kV with an electron current of 100 pA. After EBL, the sample was developed with ZED-N50 for 60 s and ZED-B for 10 s. Then, RIE (RIE-101iPH, Samco Inc.) was used to etch the MoOCl2 with SF6 gas. After RIE, the EB resist was cleanly removed using the lift-off (DMAC) process at 70°C for 20–30 min, without ultrasonication. Finally, the sample was cleaned with acetone and methanol. We also fabricated some samples with a hard mask of several-nm Ti. For those samples, a helicon sputtering (MPS-4000C1/HC1, ULVAC) and an ultrasonic lift-off process were used before the RIE process.

For twist metasurfaces, MoOCl2 flakes with similar thickness were pre-selected, and the twist angle was pre-defined during the transfer process. The surface of the lower MoOCl2 was cleaned to remove residue PDMS. After transfer, the sample was annealed under vacuum at 100–130°C for 20 min. These steps were intended to reduce interlayer bubbles. The subsequent steps are the same as those for single–disk metasurfaces with EB resist as a mask.

For MoOCl2 MIM metasurfaces, silica substrates with gold markers were used to sputter 100 nm Au, with 2 nm Ti as the adhesion layer. Then, Al2O3 layers were grown on the substrates using atomic layer deposition (ALD) at a rate of 1 nm/10 cycles (R-200 advanced, Picosun). Then, MoOCl2 flakes were transferred onto these Al2O3/Au/SiO2 substrates. The subsequent steps are the same as those for single–disk metasurfaces with EB resist as a mask.

After sample preparations, the samples were characterized using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (SU8230, Hitachi High-Technologies), and a thickness measuring instrument (ET200, Kosaka Laboratory, Ltd.).

Spectral measurements
The resonance modes of MoOCl2 metasurfaces were characterized using transmission or reflection spectra, with a home-built optical microscopy system equipped with a photonic multichannel analyzer (PMAC7473, Hamamatsu Photonics). A linear polarizer and a 1/4 λ waveplate were used to control the polarization states. For the reflection spectra, a silver mirror was used as the reference, and calibration was performed using the reflectance of silicon to obtain the actual spectra.

PEEM measurements
The PEEM measurements were performed on a high-resolution low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM)/PEEM system (ACSPELEEM III, Elmitec GmbH). A commercial Ti:sapphire femtosecond laser (MaiTai HP, Spectra-Physics, pulse duration: 80−100 fs) operated at 690−1040 nm (2.9 W @ 820 nm) with a repetition rate of 80 MHz was used to provide a tunable laser for PEEM measurements. The pulses were focused on the sample surface at normal incidence with a spot diameter of approximately 100 μm. The polarization of the laser was controlled by a λ/2 waveplate.

Simulations
The resonance modes of MoOCl2 metasurfaces were simulated using the finite-difference time-domain method (FDTD, Ansys Lumerical), using the measured permittivity (εx, εy) and theoretical permittivity (εz). The optical properties of Au were obtained from Johnson and Christy and the refractive index of the glass substrate was set to 1.5. For twist metasurfaces, the refractive index axes were rotated using the “permittivity rotation attribute” component. The excitation light was set to normal incidence with the required polarization states. The FDTD simulations well reproduced the experimental results.

Data availability
The data supporting the findings are displayed in the main text and the supplementary information. All raw data are available from the corresponding authors upon request.

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Li et al. describes the nanofabrication and investigation of arrays of nanostructured MoOCl2 realizing both hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances as well as chiral optical responses. Hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances have never been reported prior to this work and suggest a new opportunity for controlling and modifying MoOCl2 for nanophotonic applications. They authors also demonstrate that by creating at twisted MoOCl2 sample prior to nanofabrication they can achieve extremely strong circular dichroism even in a material that is otherwise isotropic in plane. Such research into anisotropic and hyperbolic materials, such as MoOCl2, is extremely important in the nanophotonics field as efforts have turned to using natural material anisotropy in order to control material properties.
Overall the manuscript was well written, the analysis, interpretation and conclusions were largely sound. However, there are several additional major and minor points that should be addressed in revisions.
Major Points:
1. The authors should address what benefits the twisted MoOCl2 provides over chiral noble metal nanostructures.
2. The authors should be careful to note that in a biaxial medium there are always two propagating wave solutions (both extraordinary). The hyperbolic modes occur for only one root of the quartic wave equation. Do both roots play a role in the observed modes in the H-LPRs? (see Narimanov, E. E. Phys. Rev. A 98, 013818 (2018))
3. In the text the manuscript states: "Ray-like lines appear because most wavevectors are oriented along the asymptotes of the hyperbola, and their directions are determined by the open angle of the hyperbola.”
These ray-like modes seem to be attributed to “ghost modes” else where. See Narimanov, E. E. Phys. Rev. A 98, 013818 (2018) and Venturi et al. Such directional ghost modes show the unique character of having both propagating and evanescent character even without intrinsic material losses. Are the rays observed here due to the hyperbolic modes (defined by the hyperbolic isofrequency surface) or the ghost modes? I don't disagree that that these appear to be localized plasmon resonances in a hyperbolic material, the question becomes do they have truly hyperbolic dispersion or not.
4. As discussed in the supplementary information increasing R redshifts the spectra while increasing H blueshifts the spectra. Could the authors explain why increasing H would increase the energy of the hyperbolic mode? It seems that thin film models of surface plasmonic behavior could explain this in a quite straightforward fashion without needing to invoke a hyperbolic mode.
Minor Points:
1. Figures 2d and e, please clarify more in the figure itself that the spectra are being plotted versus disk radius.
2. Figure 3 is confusing. It was hard to tell which of the subpanels were which polarizations and smaller FOVs at first glance. I would recommend modifying the arrangement of the panels and perhaps being more selective on which panels are displayed in the main text.

### Reviewer 3

Comments about NCOMMS-25-92838-T
In this work, the authors report hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances in the two-dimensional material MoOCl2, which exhibits strong in-plane anisotropy, and introduce twist-induced chirality in geometrically symmetric metasurfaces. The observed plasmon resonances feature one-dimensional confinement, z-gap independence, and pronounced circular dichroism arising from twist-induced chirality. However, promising hyperbolic media are expected to exhibit high electromagnetic confinement, low energy loss, and flexible tunability under external fields. The hyperbolic MoOCl2 system does not offer any fundamentally new advantages in electromagnetic confinement, energy loss and tunability, compared with previously reported materials such as MoO3, h-BN, WTe2, Ga2O3 and black phosphorus, all of which have already been extensively studied for supporting hyperbolic polaritons. In addition, the current experimental data set is incomplete and insufficient to support the major claims making it difficult to evaluate the robustness of the conclusions. As a result, the novelty of this work appears limited for publication in Nature Communications and would be more suitable for a specialized journal.
Comments:
1. The authors claim that MoOCl₂ exhibits one-dimensional characteristics in its hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances. However, one-dimensional materials are generally composed of 1D structural units connected by weak van der Waals interactions, which is not clearly illustrated or discussed in Fig. 1a. Clarification on the structural origin of this claimed one-dimensionality is necessary.
2. In Fig. 1b, the real part of the permittivity appears to vary almost linearly with wavelength, which seems unusual for 2D materials. It would be necessary to also provide the imaginary part of the optical dielectric function, as the real and imaginary components should satisfy the Kramers–Kronig relation. Including this information would help verify the physical consistency of the presented optical data. If experimental measurements are challenging, first-principles calculations could also be provided to support and better interpret the observed results.
3. The physical origin of the observed hyperbolicity should be clarified. In particular, the respective roles of interband and intraband transitions, which are crucial for producing strong optical anisotropy and hyperbolic dispersion, need to be discussed in greater detail. Providing this analysis would help elucidate the microscopic mechanism underlying the reported hyperbolic behavior. Similar discussions has been reported in Nat Commun 11, 1158 (2020).
4. The presented hyperbolic isofrequency contours appear incomplete. Additional data points at a wider range of frequencies should be included to clearly illustrate the frequency range over which hyperbolicity occurs, as well as the transition from elliptic to hyperbolic dispersion. This would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the material's optical anisotropy and dispersion characteristics.
5. The wavelength ratio of the hyperbolic in-plane dispersion to the corresponding free-space photon wavelength (i.e., electromagnetic confinement) should be provided, along with the propagation length and lifetime of the hyperbolic polaritons. These parameters are essential for quantitatively evaluating the performance and quality of hyperbolic materials.
6. Plasmon hyperbolic materials often exhibit higher losses, a short discussion on loss mechanisms in MoOCl2, including thickness dependence and Q-factor of H-LPRs would help readers assess performance limits and potential device implications.
7. The manuscript states that chirality is robust to thickness mismatch and fabrication variations, but it would help to quantify the tolerance (percent-level deviations in thickness or twist angle).
8. Can the authors elaborate on the microscopic origin of the twist-induced chirality, possibly through a brief tensor-transformation argument for the rotated permittivity?
9. Would chirality persist in multilayer twist stacks (beyond bilayers), and if so, does the effective thickness model remain applicable?

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript reports the discovery and experimental demonstration of the hyperbolic localized plasmon resonances (H-LPRs) in the anisotropic two-dimensional van der Waals material MoOCl₂. H-LPRs originate from the intrinsic in-plane anisotropic permittivity (metallic along the Mo-O chain axis, dielectric in orthogonal directions), leading to hyperbolic iso-frequency contours. H-LPRs exhibit three important properties: one-dimensional resonance, Z-gap independence and twist-induced chirality. These properties are validated through far-field spectroscopy, near-field photoemission electron microscopy imaging, and comprehensive simulations. Overall, the manuscript is clearly written and the topic is of interest. However, prior to publication, several issues should be addressed:
1.The authors attribute Z-gap independence to the matching permittivity between MoOCl₂ and Al₂O₃. Could a more quantitative analysis be provided to explain why the high-k gap modes is strongly suppressed, leading to insensitivity to gap thickness?
2.For anisotropic 2D materials (e.g., α-MoO₃), studies have shown that significant circular dichroism can be achieved by directly stacking two flakes with a twist angle. If two pristine, unpatterned MoOCl₂ flakes are stacked with a twist, what would be the expected CD value of such a system? Is fabricating a metasurface to obtain H-LPRs a necessary condition for achieving the strong chirality?
3.To demonstrate hyperbolic properties, the inset in Fig. 1b only emphasizes the hyperbolic in-plane isofrequency contours (xy-plane). However, in Fig. 1f, the ray-like electric field distribution, which is a hallmark of hyperbolicity, appears to be stronger out-of-plane (xz-plane). Does this suggest that the one-dimensional resonance characteristic stems from both in-plane and out-of-plane hyperbolic properties?

5.In the introduction, when discussing hyperbolic polaritons, the reviewer recommends citing Nature Communications 11, 1158 (2020), which reports WTe₂ as another hyperbolic material and is relevant to the context.
